summary: Defines MIB objects for managing Ethernet-like interfaces, and it adds information useful for managing 10 gigabit per second Ethernet interfaces. It obsoletes RFC 2665. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Every network jack has dials and meters a manager can read. This document refreshes that list of dials so it also covers the newer, much faster 10 gigabit connections.

questions: what is the ethernet-like interface mib
which iftype should ethernet interfaces use
why do 10 gigabit ethernet interfaces need 64-bit counters
subtitle: The SNMP counters and settings that let a network manager watch Ethernet ports from 10 Mb/s up to 10 Gb/s.

tldr.problem: Network managers need a standard way to read statistics and status from Ethernet interfaces, and Ethernet kept getting faster, with 10 Gb/s now added to the IEEE 802.3 standard.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a MIB module (EtherLike-MIB) of SNMP objects for Ethernet-like interfaces. It extends the generic Interfaces MIB with Ethernet error counters, duplex and PAUSE flow-control information, and 64-bit counters for fast links.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2665 and adds 10 Gb/s support. It also tightens the rule that every Ethernet-like interface reports the single ifType value ethernetCsmacd(6).

today: RFC 3635 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 2665, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 3635 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing Ethernet-like interfaces. A MIB is a virtual information store of managed objects, and its objects are generally read and changed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). The module is written in SMIv2.

The document obsoletes RFC 2665. Its main update is management information for 10 Gigabit per second (Gb/s) Ethernet. The RFC says that Ethernet will keep evolving, so this document is one stage in that evolution and may be revised or replaced.

The definitions are based on Section 30 and Annex 30A of IEEE Std. 802.3, 2002 Edition, as amended by IEEE Std. 802.3ae-2002. The IEEE document describes when, where and how the MAC attributes are measured. Attributes already covered by MIB-2 or the Interfaces MIB, such as octet counts, frame counts, promiscuous status and the MAC address, are not defined again here.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a car dashboard. This document lists the gauges for a network plug so that any manager's computer can read them in the same way, even for the newest fast plugs.

sections.title: How It Fits With the Interfaces MIB
sections.content:
The Interfaces MIB (RFC 2863) requires each media-specific MIB to clarify certain areas. Section 3.2 of this RFC does that for Ethernet. There are no virtual circuits on this medium, so that area does not apply. Normally there are no sublayers either, but link aggregation and the 802.3 WAN Interface Sublayer (RFC 3637) can use the ifStackTable.

The ifType rules are strict. All Ethernet-like interfaces MUST return ethernetCsmacd(6), whatever the speed or encapsulation, and MUST NOT return fastEther(62), fastEtherFX(69) or gigabitEthernet(117). The values iso88023Csmacd(7) and starLan(11) are deprecated. Management applications should still expect the old values from older implementations. The exact flavor of Ethernet comes from ifSpeed and from ifMauType in the 802.3 MAU MIB (RFC 3636), whose implementation is REQUIRED.

Other mappings are spelled out too. ifMtu must reflect the MTU actually in use as seen by the MAC client interface, and the standard MTU is 1500 octets. For speeds of 1000 Mb/s or less, ifSpeed gives the speed in bits per second and ifHighSpeed gives it in millions of bits per second. Above that, ifSpeed reports 4,294,967,295 and ifHighSpeed is 10,000 for 10 Gb/s LAN interfaces and 9,294 for the 10 Gb/s MAC over an OC-192 PHY. Neither value is doubled for full duplex.
sections.plainLanguage: There is already a general gauge board for every kind of network plug. This part says how each general gauge should be read for an Ethernet plug, and that every Ethernet plug must wear the same name tag.

sections.title: Counting Octets and Packets
sections.content:
The RFC spends real effort on how Interfaces MIB counters relate to the IEEE 802.3 counters, because the two do not match exactly. The IF-MIB octet counters (ifInOctets, ifOutOctets and their high-capacity versions) count all octets in valid frames including the MAC header and FCS, but not the preamble, start of frame delimiter or extension octets. They leave out collided or failed transmit attempts and invalid received frames.

The packet counters count requests from a higher layer, not successful transmissions. Packets counted by ifOutErrors or ifOutDiscards are therefore counted in the outgoing packet counters but not in aFramesTransmittedOK. MAC Control frames come from a sublayer inside the interface, so they show up in the octet counters and in the IEEE frame counters but not in the IF-MIB packet counters.

The RFC gives its reason for that choice. MAC control frames are normally sent as multicast packets, and in many networks they can greatly outnumber real multicast data. Counting them would drown out the multicast counters and make them much less useful. The RFC also gives rough formulas relating the two counter families, for example ifInOctets = aOctetsReceivedOK + (18 * aFramesReceivedOK).
sections.plainLanguage: Two people count the same toy cars in different ways: one counts cars on the road, the other counts cars that were handed to them. This part explains who counts what, so the numbers can be compared.

sections.title: The Ethernet-Specific Objects
sections.content:
The module sits under mib-2 35 as etherMIB, with the dot3 subtree under transmission 7. Its main tables are:

  • dot3StatsTable: one row per Ethernet-like interface, indexed by dot3StatsIndex (the same value as ifIndex). It holds error counters such as dot3StatsAlignmentErrors, dot3StatsFCSErrors, dot3StatsLateCollisions and dot3StatsSymbolErrors, plus dot3StatsDuplexStatus and the rate control objects.
  • dot3CollTable: a histogram of how many frames saw a given number of collisions (1 to 16). Implementing it is optional.
  • dot3ControlTable and dot3PauseTable: MAC Control and PAUSE flow-control information. dot3PauseAdminMode is the only read-write object in the module.
  • dot3HCStatsTable: 64-bit versions of the error counters that apply to full-duplex interfaces.

dot3StatsDuplexStatus reports unknown(1), halfDuplex(2) or fullDuplex(3). Duplex is actually controlled through the MAU MIB. The RFC accepts the redundancy with ifMauType because it lets an application learn the duplex mode without knowing every ifMauType value. The new dot3StatsRateControlAbility and dot3StatsRateControlStatus objects cover the Rate Control function in 10 Gb/s WAN applications.

The old dot3StatsEtherChipSet object is deprecated. The RFC says implementation feedback showed it was more useful in theory than in practice, and the chipset OID values live in RFC 2666.
sections.plainLanguage: The dials are grouped into drawers: one for counting mistakes, one for crashes between messages, one for the stop-and-wait signal, and one for extra-big counters that will not run out.

sections.title: Fast Links and 64-bit Counters
sections.content:
The headline change is 10 Gb/s support. The RFC points out that for interfaces running at 10 Gb/s a 32-bit counter can roll over in less than 5 minutes if it is incrementing at its maximum rate. That can be shorter than a management station's poll cycle, so information would be lost.

The fix is a set of new 64-bit counters. The change log lists dot3HCControlInUnknownOpcodes, dot3HCInPauseFrames, dot3HCOutPauseFrames and six dot3HCStats error counters. The descriptions tell managers to poll the 64-bit version on interfaces running at 10 Gb/s or faster.

The interface-level high-capacity counters (ifHCInOctets and ifHCOutOctets) are required for interfaces that can operate at 20 Mb/s or faster. The packet counters (such as ifHCInUcastPkts) are required for interfaces capable of 640 Mb/s or faster, even if the interface is currently running slower.
sections.plainLanguage: A small odometer rolls back to zero very quickly on a rocket-fast car. So the very fast plugs get a giant odometer that takes ages to roll over.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Only one object has read-write access: dot3PauseAdminMode. Changing it alters flow control on an interface, which may drop packets or send flow control packets to a link partner that will not understand them. Either could hurt network performance.

Readable objects may also be sensitive. The deprecated dot3StatsEtherChipSet could let an intruder learn which vendor's equipment is in use, and the statistics describe how links behave. The RFC says to control even GET and NOTIFY access and possibly to encrypt the values sent over SNMP.

It also says SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. It is RECOMMENDED to deploy SNMPv3 with cryptographic security, and deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the dials only show numbers, but one lets you turn a knob. Only trusted people should be allowed near that knob, and the numbers should not be shouted across the room.

sections.title: IANA and the ifType Values
sections.content: The RFC defines no new IANA name space. It does ask for comments in the existing IANAifType-MIB module. The values iso88023Csmacd(7) and starLan(11) are marked deprecated, and fastEther(62), fastEtherFX(69) and gigabitEthernet(117) are marked obsolete. In each case the comment points to ethernetCsmacd(6) as the value to use instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The old name tags are crossed out in the official list, with a note saying which single tag everyone should wear now.
